title: When the Harvest Falls
premise: Marguerite Quintana has spent twelve years mapping the unmapped tunnels beneath the drowned town of Harrow's Bend, telling themselves the scratching behind the walls is water, rats, settling stone. When a city excavation crew breaches a door sealed from the inside, the town's founders' pact is broken, and the thing in the well begins to refill, reclaiming the descendants of those who sealed it away. Marguerite learns the founders didn't imprison a monster—they imprisoned their own crimes, and the ritual to reseal it requires a confession the surviving families will kill to keep buried. In the flooded dark beneath the town, Marguerite completes the ritual by speaking their own twelve-year-old complicity aloud, drowning the truth permanently at the cost of their maps, their memories of the tunnels, and nearly their life.
about_author: Wendell Coldharbour is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing sealed town records in the American Midwest before turning to horror. Their fiction is known for bureaucratic dread and the quiet horror of what small towns agree not to remember.

chapters.title: Survey Discrepancies
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Twelve years of tunnel mapping condensed into one obsessive night as they compare their hand-drawn surveys against the county's official records and find a corridor that appears on neither. The beat is quiet unease—the first admission that the maps disagree with reality, not with each other.

chapters.title: The Crew Arrives
chapters.summary: Marguerite watches from a storm drain as the excavation crew breaks ground on the old cannery lot, directly above their secret corridor. POV shifts to crew foreman Dale Okonkwo, who notices Marguerite and logs a 'trespasser' report. The beat is intrusion—Marguerite's invisibility ending in real time.

chapters.title: What the Ground Gave Back
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. The excavator bites into dressed stone forty feet down—foundation-grade masonry where no building should be—and the crew unearths a door, its iron handle fused, the seal marks on the INSIDE. Dale pockets a brass token found wedged in the frame. The beat is professional confidence curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, interwoven flashbacks to their first descent at nineteen, when the scratching started. Each noise they ever rationalized replays, and each rationalization now sounds like a lie they chose. The beat is retrospective horror—the reader realizes Marguerite has always known.

chapters.title: The Descendants' Meeting
chapters.summary: Marguerite attends the town hall emergency meeting incognito. Six founding-family descendants—Aldrich, Vane, the Merrick sisters—argue about 'the well' with a vocabulary too practiced for a first emergency. Marguerite recognizes the brass token from Dale's photo in the local paper. The beat is the horror of institutional calm.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. They descend through their corridor to the breached door and find the crew's floodlights abandoned, the excavation silent, and scratch marks on the inside of the door matching the ones in their walls—made by fingernails, not claws. The beat is vertigo: the thing behind the door was human once, maybe.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Dale's POV, fragmented and deteriorating. Water rising in the shaft that shouldn't exist; the brass token growing warm; his crew members hearing their own names in the pump noise. He returns to the door and finds it open. The beat is a man realizing his report will never be believed, then realizing he won't live to file it.

chapters.title: Aldrich's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marguerite breaks into the Aldrich family archive and finds the founders' ledger: names, payments, and a ritual diagram keyed to the well, with the final page torn out. The last intact entry lists the 'kept'—people the founders sealed away to protect their fortunes. The beat is righteous fury meeting fear.

chapters.title: The Merrick Sisters
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts the Merrick sisters, who admit the families have maintained the seal for six generations and that the ritual requires a descendant's confession—spoken into the well as the water rises. They refuse; their family name depends on the silence. The beat is power choosing corruption over truth.

chapters.title: Missing Persons, Old and New
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, cross-referencing the ledger's 'kept' names against a century of disappearances, then against the missing excavation crew. The pattern is airtight and damning. The beat is cold clarity—justice outside the law begins as an act of bookkeeping.

chapters.title: What Took Dale
chapters.summary: Marguerite descends to find Dale alive but changed, standing waist-deep in the rising well water, reciting the ledger entries in the founders' voices. He begs Marguerite to let the water take him. The beat is horror as mercy—and the first hint the well doesn't punish the guilty, it collects the complicit.

chapters.title: The Vane Counter-Ritual
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The Vane family, the poorest of the six, secretly approaches Marguerite: they'll help complete the ritual, but they want the ledger public afterward. Marguerite must decide whether justice and survival can share an exit. The beat is alliance forged in bad faith on both sides.

chapters.title: The Scratching Explained
chapters.summary: A devastating midpoint reveal: Marguerite follows the wall-scratching to its source and finds the corridor they've mapped for twelve years is lined with the 'kept,' still sealed in the stone, still aware—and Marguerite's mapping, their trespass, their presence has been the only company they've had. The beat is guilt detonating.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Complicity
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, flashback chapter. At nineteen, they found a sealed alcove with a hand pressing through the mortar and ran, told no one, and kept coming back—for the thrill, the maps, the secret that made them special. The beat is the protagonist confronting the truth: they weren't an innocent witness. They were a voyeur.

chapters.title: The Families Close Ranks
chapters.summary: The Aldriches and Vanes discover the alliance; the town cuts the power to the cannery district and files a restraining order naming Marguerite, using the law as a weapon of silence. The beat is institutional power revealing itself—justice outside the law because the law is on the other side.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Marguerite recovers the ledger's torn final page from the Merrick house: the ritual's completion requires the confession of a descendant AND a witness—one who saw and stayed silent. The page names a Quintana. Marguerite's family were founders' clerks; their twelve years of listening were inherited. The beat is identity collapsing into inheritance.

chapters.title: Rising
chapters.summary: The well accelerates; water floods the lower town, and the sealed dead begin speaking through the drains in the voices of the townsfolk's own ancestors. The Vanes waver; one sister Merrick defects with the ritual's missing physical component. The beat is the town's buried past becoming literally audible.

chapters.title: Descent with Confession
chapters.summary: Marguerite enters the well chamber as the water climbs, the defected Merrick holding the door, the Vanes gone back on their word. Marguerite begins the founders' liturgy but replaces the founders' scripted denial with true confession—naming the kept, naming their own silence. The beat is terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: The Kept Answer
chapters.summary: The sealed dead rise from the walls to hear the confession; the well's thing reveals itself as the accumulated guilt of six generations, wearing the faces of everyone the town failed. It offers Marguerite a trade: their memories of the tunnels in exchange for the seal. The beat is the climax's moral fulcrum.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Gives
chapters.summary: Marguerite accepts—confessing fully, surrendering twelve years of maps and memories—and speaks the closing words as the water seals the door from the inside once more, this time with truth instead of silence behind it. The beat is sacrifice as justice: the ritual completed not to bury the past, but to finally acknowledge it.

chapters.title: After the Water
chapters.summary: Marguerite wakes on the cannery lot with no memory of the tunnels, holding a map they can't read and a brass token they don't recognize. The town's water recedes; the families scatter; the ledger surfaces anonymously online. The beat is hollow, ambiguous peace—justice done by someone who can no longer remember doing it.

chapters.title: The New Survey
chapters.summary: Final chapter, close third on a young explorer years later, finding Marguerite's maps in an archive and feeling, faintly, the urge to check a corridor that appears on no survey. In the last lines, Marguerite—older, at peace, uncomprehending—pauses at a wall where something scratches once, gently, like a thank-you. The beat is memory's return as haunting, and grace.
